# Resume Screening & Ranking

Score and rank candidate resumes against a job description with a per-criterion rationale for every score — and, unlike most "AI resume screener" demos, an actual measurement of whether the scorer is sensitive to a candidate's name.

**Live demo (UI):** _pending — Streamlit Community Cloud deploy needs the account holder's Streamlit login_
**Live API:** _pending — Render deploy needs the account holder's Render account_
**API docs:** `<api-url>/docs` once deployed (FastAPI auto-generated)

## The problem

A recruiter or hiring manager screening a stack of resumes against a job description does it by skimming, under time pressure, with no consistent rubric between candidates and no record of *why* one resume beat another. That's slow, inconsistent between reviewers, and produces no audit trail if a rejected candidate ever asks why. This tool applies a fixed, weighted rubric to every candidate against the same job description, in seconds, with a written rationale per criterion — and reports honestly on how sensitive that rubric actually is to identity signals (a candidate's name, a university's prestige connotation) it shouldn't be sensitive to.

## Architecture

```
resume.txt --------> Claude structured output --------> Candidate
(free text)          (extraction, schema-constrained)    {skills, years, roles, education}
                                                                |
job_description.txt ----------------------------------------> Claude structured output
                                                                (rubric scoring, name-blind
                                                                 by construction — the Candidate's
                                                                 `name` field never reaches this
                                                                 call, and any literal name
                                                                 occurrence is scrubbed from
                                                                 free text too)
                                                                |
                                                                v
                                                      CandidateScore
                                                      {per-criterion 1-5 + rationale,
                                                       weighted_total}
                                                                |
                                                       rank_candidates()
                                                       (job_id-seeded tie-break —
                                                        ties are common, not rare,
                                                        at this rubric's resolution)
```

- **Backend:** FastAPI. `POST /extract` (resume text → structured `Candidate`), `POST /score` (resume + JD → `CandidateScore`, extracts then scores internally), `/health`, `/docs`.
- **Extraction & scoring:** direct Claude structured-output calls (`client.messages.parse`), not RAG and not an autonomous agent — deliberately a third distinct pattern from this portfolio's other two projects (a citation-grounded RAG assistant, and an autonomous GitHub-triage agent). No vector DB, no tool-use loop.
- **Name-blind scoring by default:** the rubric scorer never sees the candidate's name — not because the field is omitted (that alone isn't enough; a resume can restate a name inside a bullet), but because free text is regex-scrubbed of the candidate's name and its individual tokens (case-insensitive, word-boundary-aware) before the scoring prompt is built. `include_name=True` exists only as an opt-in for the bias eval below, never in the production path.
- **UI:** Streamlit — paste a job description, upload resumes, get a ranked table with expandable per-criterion rationale.
- **Synthetic corpus:** every resume and job description in this repo is generated by a deterministic, seeded Python template (`scripts/generate_resumes.py`), not scraped or LLM-generated — real resume datasets carry real PII even when marketed "anonymized," and a template guarantees a resume can be held byte-identical except for one swapped field, which the bias eval needs and neither a scraped nor an LLM-generated corpus can promise.

## Guardrails

- **PII handling:** resume/JD text is never persisted to disk by this app and never appears in logs or error responses — every exception in the extraction/scoring path is re-raised with only a candidate/job id in its message (`from None`, so a chained exception can't leak the original text either). The structured-output SDK call itself can raise a `pydantic.ValidationError` whose message quotes the model's raw (invalid) output — caught and re-wrapped before it can propagate. FastAPI's default 422 handler is overridden to strip the `input` field it would otherwise echo back. The log formatter emits only the exception *type*, never a formatted traceback — and uvicorn's own loggers are explicitly routed through that same formatter, since by default they bypass it entirely and would log a re-raised exception (with any text it carries) in plain text instead.
- **Rate limiting:** keyed on the real connection IP by default (`TRUST_PROXY=false`); only trusts `X-Forwarded-For` behind an actual reverse proxy, and only reads the *rightmost* entry even then — an earlier version of this project's Dockerfile passed uvicorn a proxy-trust flag that silently contradicted this logic (uvicorn trusts the *leftmost* XFF entry), which would have made the "no proxy" fallback spoofable; caught by rebuilding and testing the actual container, not by reading the code.
- **Body size limit:** requests are fully buffered and capped (32KB) before Pydantic validation ever runs, not just field-level `max_length` — a large body can OOM a container before validation gets a chance to reject it.
- **Rubric weight integrity:** the four rubric weights are checked to sum to 1.0 at import time with a real `raise`, not a bare `assert` — assertions are silently stripped under `python -O`, which would remove the check exactly in an optimized deploy.
- **No `cost_guard` middleware:** a sibling project in this portfolio has one, and its own README documents it as resetting on every restart — not a real backstop. The actual spend cap here is a hard limit set on the Anthropic API key itself (Anthropic console), not application code.
- **Client timeouts:** the Anthropic SDK's default (600s, with retries) is too long for a sync endpoint running in a limited threadpool — a handful of hung upstream calls could otherwise take `/health` down too. Capped at 60s.

## Eval results

**Status: harness built, reviewed (2-3 Opus rounds per phase), and dry-run verified — not yet run against the live API.** Both eval scripts print an exact call-count estimate and refuse to spend anything without `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` and an explicit `--run` flag:

```
python -m eval.run_eval        # prints: 121 calls, ~$1.90 (dry run, no requests made)
python -m eval.run_eval --run  # actually runs it, writes eval/results.md

python -m eval.bias_eval       # prints: 215 calls, ~$3.40 (dry run, no requests made)
python -m eval.bias_eval --run # actually runs it, writes eval/bias_results.md
```

This section will be replaced with the real numbers once those run — no placeholder numbers are committed in their place.

### Methodology (what each eval actually measures)

- **Extraction accuracy** (`eval/run_eval.py`): the synthetic corpus's generation script also emits the *factual* ground truth it used (skills, years, roles, education — deliberately not the quality-relevant attributes below, so this can't leak into the ranking eval) — extraction is scored against that directly, no LLM judge needed.
- **Ranking quality**: ground truth is one non-recruiter labeler (a subagent, in this build) reading the actual resume/JD text — blind to the corpus's hidden generation parameters — ranked *within* seniority tier per job, not across tiers, since tier itself would otherwise be a generation-time confound. Headline metric is per-tier top-k precision and pairwise agreement; Kendall tau-b is reported as a secondary number only (at a handful of candidates per tier, it has no usable confidence interval). Two baselines, not one: deterministic TF-IDF cosine similarity, and a rubric-free single-call "just rank these" LLM baseline — the second isolates whether the structured rubric earns its extra cost over a bare LLM judgment, which the keyword-only baseline can't tell you (it only proves "LLM beats grep," which isn't in question).
- **Corpus quality gradient**: since tier alone gives the ranking eval nothing to grade beyond keyword/experience overlap, four tier-independent attributes are randomly assigned per resume (quantified vs. vague achievement bullets, stable vs. job-hopping tenure, title progression vs. flat, degree-field match vs. mismatch) — visible in the rendered text, not encoded as a hidden label, so a rubric judge and a TF-IDF baseline genuinely have different signal to work with.
- **Bias eval** (`eval/bias_eval.py`): two arms, not the three the original plan sketched. Current Claude models have no determinism knob (`temperature`/`top_p`/`top_k` are removed), so every delta is measured against a same-input noise floor (n≥3 reruns) rather than a bare single-sample comparison, floored at 0.10 — the smallest single rubric criterion's weight, so a one-point flip on that criterion alone sits exactly at the detection floor, not below it.
  - **Arm 1 (name swap, name-visible scorer)** — the actual bias measurement: does the model score a candidate differently when only the name changes, with the name visible to it? Uses paired names from the Bertrand & Mullainathan (2004) audit-study convention.
  - **Arm 2 (university swap, name-blind scorer)** — the *required* measurement, not optional: since the production scorer is name-blind by construction, a name swap through it can only ever remeasure noise (proven as an exact offline assertion, not spent as ~126 live calls — see `tests/test_scoring.py::test_blind_serialization_identical_across_name_swap`). University text isn't scrubbed, so this measures real residual sensitivity to a prestige-connotation swap while the name stays hidden.
  - Rank-flip count (named in the original design) isn't reported: each rep swaps one candidate against one job, so there's no second candidate to flip rank against — a real scope gap, disclosed rather than silently dropped.

## Known limitations (deliberate scope cuts)

- **Synthetic corpus only.** No real resumes were used, for the PII and bias-eval-control reasons above — but that also means eval numbers describe how well the system handles *this* synthetic distribution, not real-world resume messiness (inconsistent formatting, OCR errors from scanned PDFs, non-US resume conventions).
- **One non-recruiter labeler** for ranking ground truth — a genuine limitation the plan disclosed upfront, not discovered after the fact.
- **Bias eval scope**: a narrow name/university-text sensitivity proxy on a synthetic corpus, explicitly not a full fairness audit. It measures score sensitivity to two specific swapped attributes, not disparate impact on real hiring outcomes.
- **Rightmost-`X-Forwarded-For` rate limiting** assumes exactly one proxy hop appends the true client IP once deployed — unverified without an actual Render deployment; documented as a post-deploy check (log the real header shape once) rather than assumed correct.
- **No resume file upload beyond .txt** — no PDF/DOCX parsing. A real product would need that; this demo accepts pasted or `.txt`-uploaded plain text only, to keep the extraction surface to what Claude's structured output actually needs to see.

## Deploying

1. **API (Render):** push to a repo Render can see, point a new Web Service at it (`render.yaml` is a Blueprint — Render reads it automatically). Set `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` in the Render dashboard (never committed — `sync: false` in `render.yaml`). **Set a spend limit on the API key itself in the Anthropic console** — that's the real budget backstop, not application code (see Guardrails above).
2. **Post-deploy check:** log the real `X-Forwarded-For` header shape once (a temporary debug log line, or check Render's own request logs) to confirm it's actually one hop before trusting `TRUST_PROXY=true`'s rightmost-entry logic — see the "Known limitations" note above and the docstring in `app/middleware/rate_limit.py`.
3. **UI (Streamlit Community Cloud):** point it at `ui/streamlit_app.py` (Streamlit Cloud finds `ui/requirements.txt` automatically since it's in the entrypoint's directory). **Set `API_URL` in the app's Secrets** to the deployed Render URL — without it, the UI silently falls back to `localhost` and every request fails with an opaque connection error.

## Running locally

```bash
python -m venv .venv && source .venv/bin/activate  # or .venv\Scripts\activate on Windows
pip install -r requirements.txt
cp .env.example .env  # fill in ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

python scripts/generate_resumes.py          # regenerate the synthetic corpus (already committed)
python scripts/generate_job_descriptions.py

uvicorn app.main:app --reload                # API on :8000
streamlit run ui/streamlit_app.py            # UI, separate terminal (needs `pip install -r ui/requirements.txt`)
```

Docker (matches the deployed image):
```bash
docker build -t resume-screening-ai .
docker run -p 8000:8000 -e ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=... resume-screening-ai
```

## Tests

```bash
pytest -q   # 63 passed, 2 skipped (the 2 are live-API smoke tests, gated on a real ANTHROPIC_API_KEY)
```

Every non-trivial code path (extraction invariants, scoring math, name-blind scrubbing, tie-break behavior, eval metrics, bias-noise statistics, API error handling) has an offline test that runs with zero API calls — `tests/conftest.py` sets a dummy API key so `app/main.py` can import for testing without a real one, and a `has_real_api_key()` helper keeps the two genuine live-smoke tests from misfiring against that dummy value.

## Engineering notes

This project was built with a per-phase review loop: each phase (data generation, extraction, scoring, quality eval, bias eval, API+UI, deploy config) was drafted, then reviewed by an independent Opus pass against the actual running code — not just the diff — until SATISFIED. Real bugs the loop caught, not just style nits:

- A `pydantic.ValidationError` raised *inside* `client.messages.parse()` (not just readable from its result afterward) quoted the model's raw output, including a candidate's name — a live PII leak the `stop_reason`-only guard in an earlier version couldn't have caught, since that check never runs when the error path is a raised exception, not a normal return.
- A "job-hopping" tenure attribute in the synthetic-resume generator that, due to a fixed role count being only shuffled rather than actually varied, reliably rendered as its *opposite* — two short stints plus one role holding 79-95% of the candidate's tenure.
- A rate-limiter tie-break bug: `rank_candidates`' ties (the common case, not rare, given the rubric's limited resolution) resolved in whatever order candidates were passed in — which was always Phase 1's manifest order, itself built category-then-tier — so every tie silently favored junior candidates. Fixed with a job-id-seeded shuffle before sorting.
- A Dockerfile flag (`--proxy-headers --forwarded-allow-ips='*'`) added on the assumption it would pair correctly with the app's own rate-limit trust logic — it didn't; uvicorn trusts the *leftmost* X-Forwarded-For entry, the app's logic trusts the *rightmost*, and the flag would have silently made the "no proxy" fallback spoofable. Found by rebuilding and testing the actual container with forged headers, not by reading the code.
- uvicorn's own loggers bypass the app's PII-safe JSON log formatter by default (separate logger, separate handler, `propagate=False`) — an unhandled exception re-raised past the app's own catch-all handler would have logged its full traceback in plain text regardless of the formatter fix above it. Proven live with a fake name/SSN string before fixing it.

See individual phase commits for the full review-round history (each commit message names what was found and fixed).
